beliefs.practice: Use a single, long-lived MongoClient instance (singleton) for the whole Node.js process, reuse it for all operations and only call client.close() on graceful shutdown.

Read the cluster connection string from an environment variable (e.g., DOCUMENTDB_URI) and never hard-code or commit it; rotate secrets via Key Vault or equivalent instead of embedding credentials in repo files.
Enable TLS/SSL in the MongoDB connection string (ssl=true or tls=true) and require certificate validation rather than disabling it, to protect credentials and data in transit.
Configure the driver connection pool size (e.g., maxPoolSize) to match expected concurrency and avoid one-client-per-request patterns — keep pool size tuned to the Node.js app's concurrency profile.

Implement robust transient-failure handling: retry on network errors and transient server errors with exponential backoff + jitter, and handle server throttling (429) specially respecting any Retry-After/x-ms-retry-after headers.

Provision throughput/compute appropriate to vector search workloads (higher RU/s or larger compute tiers) or enable autoscale; monitor consumed RU and increase capacity before throttling becomes common.

When storing vectors, use a typed binary/float representation (Float32 array) rather than JSON strings, and keep a documented 'dimension' field so index creation and retrieval use the correct dimensionality.

Create a dedicated vector index with explicit parameters (index type HNSW or DiskANN and tuned parameters like M, efConstruction, efSearch or IVF nlist) appropriate to data size and latency requirements, instead of relying on a default index.

Filter by cheap metadata first (e.g., article type, date, client segment) using standard B-tree indexes, then run the vector nearest-neighbors search on the candidate set (metadata-then-vector pattern).
Create conventional indexes on all fields used for equality or sort filters (e.g., articleId, tenantId, createdAt) and mark any unique keys explicitly (unique: true) to avoid collection scans.

Do not store unlimited conversation history in the database unbounded; enforce an upper bound (max messages), TTL, or perform periodic summarization/compaction before saving in-memory agent memory to the DB.

When seeding or testing, use deterministic, versioned embeddings and record the embed-model version used; in production ensure embedding model changes are handled via reindexing or model-version fields.
Avoid returning full vector payloads in normal queries — project out vector fields unless you need to compute similarity client-side; only fetch vector data for recomputation or reindexing jobs.
Make index creation idempotent: check existing indexes via listIndexes and only create missing ones; perform index creation during maintenance windows or with throttle controls for large datasets.

Cap document sizes and avoid very large single documents (e.g., don't embed excessively large conversation transcripts or entire portfolios), instead store long text as separate documents and reference by id.
Monitor and log request charge / RU consumption per operation (or equivalent metric) and surface slow queries/expensive vector-search calls so you can tune indexes and partitioning.
Use pagination (limit + skip or range queries with a stable sort key) for listing results; avoid large skip values for performance — prefer range queries (createdAt, _id) for deep pagination.

If using Azure-managed services, prefer Azure Key Vault + Managed Identity for credential access instead of process environment variables; fall back to env vars only for local dev with .env.example placeholders.
Record and version schema of stored documents (fields, vector dim, metadata) and include migration paths for schema changes and reindexing when vector dimension or metadata shape changes.

For local development and automated tests, keep seed scripts idempotent: check for existing documents by stable id and update/skip rather than inserting duplicates; include a --wipe option guarded by clear warnings.
